messages.subject_clean: AW: CJS model with m-array formulation with missing visits
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tomas,

I think that there is no "m-array solution" for this problem in the sense that you could have missing values somewhere in the data table. Rather as Marc has pointed out, you set in the CJS model the recapture probability to zero at the occasions without capture. Since the pattern of missing years is site specific, you would need to construct an m-array for each site and then fix the recapture to zero in a site-specific way in your model.

Kind regards

Michael

Any simple m-array solution for that, except the complicated one I sketched?

Thanks and best regards,

messages.subject: Convergence issues with goodness-of-fit Pearson residual parameters
messages.subject_clean: Convergence issues with goodness-of-fit Pearson residual parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am modeling reptile communities using JAGS, following Kery & Royle's AHM book. I'm in the final stages of creating the model, with adding the code to calculate goodness-of-fit as is described in chapter 5 and in Wearn et al. 2017.

The model runs fine, but I just cannot get the squared Pearson chi-square residual parameter for each species and site to converge.

To get good mixing for my model without the goodness-of-fit I just adjusted the priors and the initial values, but I can't see what I can change in the goodness-of-fit code. Increasing the iterations has helped a little, but it currently takes ~15 hours to run 800 000 iterations so I'd like to know if there's anything else I can adjust before upping the iterations again.

for(k in 1:nspec){          # Loop over species
    for (i in 1:nsite) {         # Loop over sites
    ynew[i,k] ~ dbin(mup[i,k], J[i]) # Simulate an ‘ideal’ dataset
    # Pearson residuals (A small non-zero value, e, prevents division by zero)
    d[i,k]<- (ysum[i,k] - mup[i,k]*J[i])/sqrt((mup[i,k]+e)*J[i]*(1-mup[i,k]-e))
    d2[i,k]<- pow(d[i,k],2)                            # observed
    dnew[i,k]<- (ynew[i,k]-mup[i,k]*J[i])/sqrt((mup[i,k]+e)*J[i]*(1-mup[i,k]-e))
    dnew2[i,k]<- pow(dnew[i,k],2)                        # expected
    }
    }

d2 is the parameter that won't converge for a number of species and sites. The non-convergence doesn't seem to be due to a specific species or site.

Any ideas on how to get good mixing would be appreciated!

Alexandra

messages.body_plain:
Dear Rahel and Elise,

dear other colleagues who answered to my desperate plea for help almost a year ago,

you may or may not remember: our problem was that in a multi-year binomial N-mixture model, as soon as we linked the abundances at a site across years in the form of a simple exponential population model, the abundance estimates became unrealistically high.

I thank you all for helping !

I have since conducted a fairly large simulation study where I simulated and analysed data sets in a factorial design to see under which conditions I would get that behaviour for the estimates of N.  Specifically, I simulated and analysed 25 10-year Nmix data sets with exponential population model  for each combination of the following cases:

-          Initial abundance low (5) or high (100)

-          With or without logit-normal or log-normal overdispersion in every parameter of the model

-          Data simulation mechanism Markovian or “extended Markov” (see Sollmann et al., Ecology, 2015)

-          Data analysis with Markovian model or with the extended Markov model of Sollmann et al., 2015

In the extended Markov model, we add a random immigration term such that the abundance in year t+1 becomes this:

N(i,t+1) ~ Poisson(N(i,t)*gamma + eps(t))

with log(eps(t)) ~ Normal(0, sigma2)

Thus, under this model, abundance at t+1 can be non-zero even if abundance at time t is zero, something which is not possible under the simpler Markov model (i.e., the simple population model with exponential growth). In the attachment is a pictorial representation of the results for the latent abundance parameters N for all 25 data sets with 10 years each (results for the cases with overdispersion are omitted).

Looking at these has convinced me that Elise’s and Rahel’s explanations for our problem were correct. Therefore, they have both won a copy of the AHM1 book, which I handed over to them rather unceremoniously in a plastic bag in St-Andrews at the recent ISEC :)

The plots show the estimated latent N’s versus the true N’s in the data simulation. Red is the 1:1 line and blue is the regression of estimate on truth.

-          On page 1 you see that if the true population dynamics is really Markovian (and an extinct population remains extinct forever), the Markov model works well, regardless of population size. (There seems to be a slight negative bias in the earlier years, but this vanishes over time.)

-          Page 2 is crucial: it shows for a small population simulated such that populations can go extinct and then later have non-zero abundance again (i.e., under extended Markov simulation), that we get exactly the picture that we got for our real bird data, where such intermittent zeroes are common in time-series of counts. The simpler Markov model greatly overestimates abundance and this becomes worse over time. In sharp contrast, a large population essentially behaves Markovian over the 10 simulated years (i.e., there were never any extinctions), and hence, the restrictive Markov model has no problems.

-          Page 3 essentially shows that when the population dynamics is truly Markov, but we adopt the more general extended Markov model of Sollmann et al., we don’t incur any costs in terms of bias.

-          Page 4 is again illuminating and should be compared with page 2. It shows that allowing a population to recover from zero abundance in the extended Markov model removes the problems with the positive bias in the estimated N’s for the case with small population size (and there was no such for the large population anyway)

(Results for the cases with overdispersion in the data generation but not in the analysis model were interesting, but not unexpected: they showed the usual bias incurred in binomial Nmix models when there is unmodelled heterogeneity in parameters, cf. recent papers by Link et al. and Duarte et al. and also Chapter 6 in AHM1 (Section 6.7). But the presence or absence of OD was not able to explain the bias in N among the different scenarios.)

Best regards  --- Marc

An: Elise Zipkin

Betreff: Re: A VERY vexing Nmix problem

Good morning,

just to add one thought along the lines of Elise's argument: the exponential growth model, as formulated, will force a population at a sampling point to remain at 0 if it ever hits 0 during the time series (because N at t+1 can never come back from 0 if N at t is 0). So that might be another mechanism forcing higher estimates of N, to avoid this "extinction". Btw, the same is true in the standard Dail-Madsen model where recruitment only depends on site-specific N at the previous time step.

Best

Rahel

On Tue, Aug 29, 2017 at 6:25 AM, Elise Zipkin <elise....@gmail.com> wrote:

Well, I'll throw in my two cents for a chance to get a copy of your new book!

I think the problem is with the structure of the model itself, the exponential growth model N_t+1~Pois(r*N_t). This is a very unrealistic growth model which will force your population to crash to zero or explode to very high numbers really, really quickly.  I believe that you can simulate data that does this (and then the model works) but I don't believe that any real population will behave according to this model for more than a few years. My guess is that this is why you say the problem gets worse as the length of the time series increases.

What to do? There are a couple of simple options to add in some sort of non-mechanistic density-dependent effects.  For example, you could change to some form of the simple discrete-time logistic growth model: N_t+1 ~ Pois (N_t + r*N_t*(K- N_t/K) ).  You could also specify the model as N_t+1 ~ Pois(lambda_t) where log(lambda_t) = a + b*N + c*N^2.  To get either of these models working in JAGS, you will likely need to standardize N by subtracting it from the approximated mean over the complete time series of the data (at least that's what we've had to do when adding density dependence into N-mixture models).  [Side note, you could try standardizing the N in your exponential growth model - subtract N from an approximated mean N over the length of the time series. My guess is that this would help some but not completely eliminate the problem.]

Of course another option would be to just use the Dail-Madsen model, which I would argue offers a little more mechanism to your modeling approach.  You could then add the density dependent mechanism (and/or covariates) onto either the survival or gains parameters directly (which I know that you already know!).

Hope this helps!

Elise

On Tue, Aug 29, 2017 at 7:50 AM, Kery Marc <marc...@vogelwarte.ch> wrote:

Dear all,

this is a call for help with a problem that really, REALLY bothers us (Rémi Fay, Michael Schaub, Marc Kéry). As a supposedly easy and interesting project at the start of his postdoc, Rémi has been fitting binomial N-mixture models to Swiss Breeding Bird Survey (MHB) data with an interest in spatio-temporal patterns in population growth rates. We specified a simple exponential population model for the abundances of successive years, such that the realized abundance at site i in year t+1 was linked with that in year t by a simple product with population growth rate r such that:

                                                N_(i,t+1) ~ Poisson(N_(i,t) * r_t)

(As a reminder, the MHB survey has 267 1km2 sites that are surveyed 2-3 times during each breeding season (essentially mid-April until end of June) and it started in 1999. )

Now the mind-boggling thing is that this dynamic model produces what we are convinced are abundance estimates that are greatly overestimated when applied to our data (results from all tested species show same behavior). In contrast, when we fit a non-dynamic model with a different expected abundance in each year, but no link between successive years (i.e., a static, multi-year N-mixture model, Royle 2004), we obtain much lower mean abundance estimates, which look much more sensible to us. But as soon as we link the abundances by a population model such as the above, the abundance estimates shoot up (see attached figure). The problem seems to get worse with increasing length of the time series (i.e., number of years) and remains whatever the combination of covariates we used to explain variation both in detection and abundance and whether we do or don't account for extra dispersion (e.g., site, site-year random effects etc).

We have run many simulations to see whether we can replicate these patterns "in the lab". However, we failed to do so: when the data-generating model matched the data-analysis model, then we obtained good inferences regardless of whether we did or did not add extra noise in the form of log- or logit-scale Gaussian residuals in any combination of the three basic parameters of the dynamic model (initial abundance lambda, growth rate r and detection probability p). Thus, it must be another feature in our data that causes the undesirable behaviour of the Nmix estimators in our dynamic model, but we are simply at a loss of imagining what that could be.

Therefore, we ask "the crowd" and hope that some of you is/are more imaginative than we were and may find the reason for this trouble. As an attachment to this mail, we send a text file that contains sample data for one species (winter wren) and another text file with R and BUGS code to fit both the static and the dynamic models in JAGS via R package jagsUI.

The first person who solves this problem that is so intruiging to us receives a copy of either our Applied hierarchical modeling (AHM1) or Bayesian Population Anaylsis (BPA) books and perhaps also a bottle of French wine. We think that this is a very vexing problem (and we imagine that it happens not only with our survey data), so any solution to it would well deserve to be written up in a paper. If you solve it, then we would be happy to let you be first author of such a methodological paper if you wish so.

Thank you very much for your interest in this.

Best regards, Rémi, Marc and Michael

    for(j in 1:J) {

    y[i,j] ~ dpois(lambda[i,j])

    }

    }

    for(j in 1:J) {

      n[j] ~ sum(y[,j])

    }

    N<- sum(w)

Dear all,

I'm fairly new to this topic, but in the near future I will have to use hierarchical models as well as GLMMs to estimate trends in population sizes. One of the things I would like to work on is the implementation of covariates, which means that I'll use information criteria and/or cross-validation for model selection, to see which covariates should remain in my models.

Now, I used one of Marc Kéry's simulated datasets (Kéry 2010 - Chapter 21) to try to implement Bayesian p-values as well as several different information criteria (DIC, WAIC, Posterior Predictive Loss (D)) and cross-validation, but I have a hard time figuring out if I'm doing it correctly. Does anyone have experience with these methods? Can anyone tell me if and where I'm making mistakes? Many thanks for your help.

Best, Jelle

###########################################################################################################

If I run the code below, it takes about 60 minutes to produce the following table:

fold bay.p c.hat bay.p.cv <http://bay.p.cv> c.hat.cv <http://c.hat.cv> DIC WAIC D non.convergence n.params.estimated

library(R2jags)

#######################
### Data generation ###
#######################
n.site <- 200                                                                 # number of sites
vege <- sort(runif(n = n.site, min = -1.5, max =1.5))                         # vegetation cover

alpha.lam <- 2                                                         # intercept
beta1.lam <- 2                                                         # linear effect of vegetation
beta2.lam <- -2                                                         # quadratic effect of vegetation
lam <- exp(alpha.lam + beta1.lam*vege + beta2.lam*(vege^2))                   # lambda

par(mfrow = c(2,1))
plot(vege, lam, main = "", xlab = "", ylab = "Expected abundance", las = 1)

N <- rpois(n = n.site, lambda = lam)                                          # simulation of abundance
table(N)                                                               # distribution of abundances across sites
sum(N > 0) / n.site                                                       # empirical occupancy

plot(vege, N, main = "", xlab = "Vegetation cover", ylab = "Realized abundance")
points(vege, lam, type = "l", lwd = 2)

par(mfrow = c(2,1))
alpha.p <- 1                                                           # intercept
beta.p <- -4                                                           # linear effect of vegetation
det.prob <- exp(alpha.p + beta.p * vege) / (1 + exp(alpha.p + beta.p * vege)) # detection probability
plot(vege, det.prob, ylim = c(0,1), main = "", xlab = "", ylab = "Detection probability")

expected.count <- N * det.prob                                                # model without error
plot(vege, expected.count, main="", xlab="Vegetation cover",
     ylab="Apparent abundance", ylim = c(0, max(N)), las = 1)
points(vege, lam, type = "l", col = "black", lwd = 2) # Truth

n.survey <- 3                                                         # number of replicate counts per site
count <- array(dim = c(n.site, n.survey))                                     # array to fill in simulated counts
for(j in 1:n.survey){
  count[,j] <- rbinom(n=n.site, size=N, prob=det.prob)                        # simulation of counts
}

site = 1:n.site                                                               # site.id <http://site.id>
max.count <- apply(count, 1, max)                                             # maximum count per site
naive.analysis <- glm(max.count ~ vege + I(vege^2), family = poisson)         # simple glm, assusuming perfect detection
summary(naive.analysis)
lin.pred <- naive.analysis$coefficients[1] + naive.analysis$coefficients[2]*vege + naive.analysis$coefficients[3] * (vege*vege)
                                                                              # linear predictor of naive analysis

par(mfrow = c(1,1))
plot(vege, max.count, main = "", xlab = "Vegetation cover",
     ylab = "Abundance or count or detection probability*max.N", ylim = c(0,max(N)), las = 1)
points(vege, lam, type = "l", col = "black", lwd = 2, lty=2)                  # true abundance
points(vege, exp(lin.pred), type = "l", col = "red", lwd = 2)                 # prediction of naive analysis
points(vege, det.prob*max(N), type="l", col="blue", lty=3)                    # detection probability * maximum abundance

###################################################################################
### Binomial mixture model, including cross-validation and information criteria ###
###################################################################################

# Model definition
bin.mix <- function(){
  # Priors
  alpha.lam ~ dunif(-10, 10)
  beta1.lam ~ dunif(-10, 10)
  beta2.lam ~ dunif(-10, 10)
  alpha.p ~ dunif(-10, 10)
  beta.p ~ dunif(-10, 10)

  # Likelihood
  for (i in indices) {
    N[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
    log(lambda[i]) <- alpha.lam + beta1.lam*vege[i] + beta2.lam*vege[i]*vege[i]
    for (j in 1:n.survey) {
      lp[i,j] <- alpha.p + beta.p * vege[i]
      p[i,j] <- exp(lp[i,j]) / (1 + exp(lp[i,j]))
    }
  }

  for (i in train.indices){
    for (j in 1:n.survey){
      count[i,j] ~ dbin(p[i,j], N[i])
    }
  }

  totalN <- sum(N[])

  # Goodness-of-fit measures
  for (i in indices) {
    for (j in 1:n.survey) {
      count.sim[i,j] ~ dbin(p[i,j], N[i])
      exp.count[i,j] <- p[i,j] * N[i]
      resid.actual[i,j] <- pow((count[i,j]-exp.count[i,j]),2) / (exp.count[i,j] + 0.5)
      resid.sim[i,j] <- pow((count.sim[i,j]-exp.count[i,j]),2) / (exp.count[i,j] + 0.5)
      ppd[i,j] <- pow(p[i,j],count[i,j]) * pow((1-p[i,j]),(N[i]-count[i,j]))
    }
  }

  fit.actual <- sum(resid.actual[train.indices,])
  fit.sim <- sum(resid.sim[train.indices,])
  c.hat <- (fit.actual+0.001) / (fit.sim+0.001)
  bay.p <- step(fit.sim - fit.actual)

  fit.cv.actual <- sum(resid.actual[test.indices,])
  fit.cv.sim <- sum(resid.sim[test.indices,])
  c.hat.cv <http://c.hat.cv> <- (fit.cv.actual+0.001) / (fit.cv.sim+0.001)
  bay.p.cv <http://bay.p.cv> <- step(fit.cv.sim - fit.cv.actual)

}

# Model settings
nc <- 3
nb <- 5000
ni <- 25000
nt <- 4
params <- c("totalN", "alpha.lam", "beta1.lam", "beta2.lam", "alpha.p", "beta.p", "fit.actual", "fit.sim",
            "c.hat", "bay.p", "fit.cv.actual", "fit.cv.sim", "bay.p.cv <http://bay.p.cv>", "c.hat.cv <http://c.hat.cv>", "ppd", "count.sim")

# Shuffle dataset for cross-validation
count.initial <- max.count+1                                                 # initial value for Bayesian model

indices <- seq(1:n.site)
set.seed(1)
shuffled.indices <- sample(indices)
shuffled.sites <- site[shuffled.indices]
shuffled.vege <- vege[shuffled.indices]
shuffled.count <- count[shuffled.indices,]
shuffled.count.initial <- count.initial[shuffled.indices]

# Run model including 10-fold cross-validation
start.time = Sys.time()                                                       # set timer

results.model <- list()                                                       # list to save results of each fold
results.ICs <- data.frame(matrix(NA, ncol=8, nrow=10))                        # data frame to save results of information criteria
colnames(results.ICs) <- c("bay.p", "c.hat", "bay.p.cv <http://bay.p.cv>", "c.hat.cv <http://c.hat.cv>", "DIC", "WAIC", "D", "non.convergence")
for (i in 1:10) {
  test.indices <- ((i-1)*round(0.1*n.site)+1):(i*round(0.1*n.site))
  train.indices <- indices[-test.indices]

  inits <- function(){list(N=shuffled.count.initial, alpha.lam=rnorm(1, 0, 1), alpha.p=rnorm(1, 0, 1),
                           beta.p=rnorm(1, 0, 1), beta1.lam=rnorm(1, 0, 1), beta2.lam=rnorm(1, 0, 1))}

  jags.data <- list(indices=indices, train.indices=train.indices, test.indices=test.indices, n.survey=n.survey,
                    vege=shuffled.vege, count=shuffled.count)

  out <- jags(jags.data, inits, params, bin.mix, n.chains=nc, n.iter=ni, n.burn = nb, n.thin=nt)

  bay.p <- out$BUGSoutput$mean$bay.p
  c.hat <- out$BUGSoutput$mean$c.hat
  bay.p.cv <http://bay.p.cv> <- out$BUGSoutput$mean$bay.p.cv <http://bay.p.cv>
  c.hat.cv <http://c.hat.cv> <- out$BUGSoutput$mean$c.hat.cv <http://c.hat.cv>

  DIC <- out$BUGSoutput$DIC

  lppd.sum <- -2*sum(log(apply(out$BUGSoutput$sims.list$ppd,2,mean)))
  pD.2 <- sum(apply(log(out$BUGSoutput$sims.list$ppd), 2, function(x) sd(x)*sd(x)))
  WAIC <- lppd.sum + pD.2

  count.sim.mean <- apply(out$BUGSoutput$sims.list$count.sim,2,mean)
  sum1 <- sum((count-count.sim.mean)^2)
  sum2 <- sum(apply(out$BUGSoutput$sims.list$count.sim,2,function(x) sd(x)*sd(x)))
  D <- sum1 + sum2

  non.convergence <- length(which(out$BUGSoutput$summary[,8]>1.1))

  results.model[[i]] <- list(summary=data.frame(out$BUGSoutput$summary))

  results.ICs[i,] <- c(bay.p, c.hat, bay.p.cv <http://bay.p.cv>, c.hat.cv <http://c.hat.cv>, DIC, WAIC, D, non.convergence)

}
end.time = Sys.time()
elapsed.time = round(difftime(end.time, start.time, units='mins'), dig = 2)
cat(paste(paste('Posterior models computed in ', elapsed.time, sep=''), ' minutes\n\n', sep=''))

Looks like differences between rjags and jagsUI (used more in the AHM book) are mucking things up.

John

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

So, I realized that my post of last Friday might have been a bit too broad in its questions, so let me specify a bit more what my exact questions are. Some help or answers on any of these issues is appreciated.

1) Is the way in which I did the cross-validation correct, with estimating the counts using only train.indices,

for (i in train.indices){

    for (j in 1:n.survey){

      count[i,j] ~ dbin(p[i,j], N[i])

    }

  }

and then calculating bay.p and c.hat for both train.indices and test.indices? Does this reflect the within-sample vs. cross-sample validation correctly?

2) I found the way to calculate the WAIC and D information criteria in two papers by Hooten & Hobbs 2015 and Gelman et al. 2014, but I'm not entirely sure I understood the mathematical formulas correctly. As it is now, I estimate ppd (pointwise posterior distribution) and count.sim (the replicate "perfect" dataset), which form the basis for these criteria, for each visit j and each site i, after which WAIC and D are based on the sum of differences over all visits and sites. However, these papers are not very specific on the topic of multiple visits and only specify that values should be summed over sites. Would it perhaps be better to first take an average over visits and then sum differences over sites? Or doesn’t that matter so much? Or does anyone have some code on how to calculate these for N-mixture and/or occupancy models?

3) In the papers mentioned above, the authors use the mathematical expression E(yi|y) and I interpreted that as what I call count.sim, i.e. the replicate “perfect” dataset that is produced by drawing from a binomial distribution, but perhaps this should be the expected count, exp.count, as calculated with p[i,j] * N[i] instead. Which one should it be?

4) Is any of the above different between N-mixture models, occupancy models and non-hierarchical logistic regressions? That is, I wonder if N represents the number of individuals, as in N-mixture models, you might get slightly different formulas than when it effectively represents the number of visits, as in occupancy. Does this have consequences for the calculation of cross-validation measures or information criteria?

5) In the table “results ICs” I produced, the null model actually has the lowest values for DIC, WAIC, and D, which I found somewhat surprising. Is this because I miscalculated something, or is this something common for these models/measures and should you just compare between different models with covariates and not with the null model?

6) Does anyone specifically have experience with model selection using N-mixture and occupancy models to estimate trends over years? Any typical order or plan to go about? I’m asking because there are several measures, such as information criteria or indicator variable selection, with or without cross-validation, but I’m going to have to do this for several hundreds of species and any extra step might take a lot of time, so I thought that maybe someone has already gone through several methods and found one way to work well.

Sorry if this is a bit much, but I thought this is the right group to ask and any ideas are welcome.

Cheers,

Jelle

> lin.pred <- naive.analysis$coefficients[1] + naive.analysis$coefficients[2]*vege + naive.analysis$coefficients[3] * (vege*vege)
>                                                                               # linear predictor of naive analysis
>
> par(mfrow = c(1,1))
> plot(vege, max.count, main = "", xlab = "Vegetation cover",
>      ylab = "Abundance or count or detection probability*max.N", ylim = c(0,max(N)), las = 1)
> points(vege, lam, type = "l", col = "black", lwd = 2, lty=2)                  # true abundance
> points(vege, exp(lin.pred), type = "l", col = "red", lwd = 2)                 # prediction of naive analysis
> points(vege, det.prob*max(N), type="l", col="blue", lty=3)                    # detection probability * maximum abundance
>
>
> ###################################################################################
> ### Binomial mixture model, including cross-validation and information criteria ###
> ###################################################################################
>
> # Model definition
> bin.mix <- function(){
>   # Priors
>   alpha.lam ~ dunif(-10, 10)
>   beta1.lam ~ dunif(-10, 10)
>   beta2.lam ~ dunif(-10, 10)
>   alpha.p ~ dunif(-10, 10)
>   beta.p ~ dunif(-10, 10)
>
>   # Likelihood
>   for (i in indices) {
>     N[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
>     log(lambda[i]) <- alpha.lam + beta1.lam*vege[i] + beta2.lam*vege[i]*vege[i]
>     for (j in 1:n.survey) {
>       lp[i,j] <- alpha.p + beta.p * vege[i]
>       p[i,j] <- exp(lp[i,j]) / (1 + exp(lp[i,j]))
>     }
>   }
>
>   for (i in train.indices){
>     for (j in 1:n.survey){
>       count[i,j] ~ dbin(p[i,j], N[i])
>     }
>   }
>
>   totalN <- sum(N[])
>
>   # Goodness-of-fit measures
>   for (i in indices) {
>     for (j in 1:n.survey) {
>       count.sim[i,j] ~ dbin(p[i,j], N[i])
>       exp.count[i,j] <- p[i,j] * N[i]
>       resid.actual[i,j] <- pow((count[i,j]-exp.count[i,j]),2) / (exp.count[i,j] + 0.5)
>       resid.sim[i,j] <- pow((count.sim[i,j]-exp.count[i,j]),2) / (exp.count[i,j] + 0.5)
>       ppd[i,j] <- pow(p[i,j],count[i,j]) * pow((1-p[i,j]),(N[i]-count[i,j]))
>     }
>   }
>
>   fit.actual <- sum(resid.actual[train.indices,])
>   fit.sim <- sum(resid.sim[train.indices,])
>   c.hat <- (fit.actual+0.001) / (fit.sim+0.001)
>   bay.p <- step(fit.sim - fit.actual)
>
>   fit.cv.actual <- sum(resid.actual[test.indices,])
>   fit.cv.sim <- sum(resid.sim[test.indices,])
>   c.hat.cv <http://c.hat.cv> <- (fit.cv.actual+0.001) / (fit.cv.sim+0.001)
>   bay.p.cv <http://bay.p.cv> <- step(fit.cv.sim - fit.cv.actual)
>
> }
>
> # Model settings
> nc <- 3
> nb <- 5000
> ni <- 25000
> nt <- 4
> params <- c("totalN", "alpha.lam", "beta1.lam", "beta2.lam", "alpha.p", "beta.p", "fit.actual", "fit.sim",
>             "c.hat", "bay.p", "fit.cv.actual", "fit.cv.sim", "bay.p.cv <http://bay.p.cv>", "c.hat.cv <http://c.hat.cv>", "ppd", "count.sim")
>
> # Shuffle dataset for cross-validation
> count.initial <- max.count+1                                                 # initial value for Bayesian model
>
> indices <- seq(1:n.site)
> set.seed(1)
> shuffled.indices <- sample(indices)
> shuffled.sites <- site[shuffled.indices]
> shuffled.vege <- vege[shuffled.indices]
> shuffled.count <- count[shuffled.indices,]
> shuffled.count.initial <- count.initial[shuffled.indices]
>
> # Run model including 10-fold cross-validation
> start.time = Sys.time()                                                       # set timer
>
> results.model <- list()                                                       # list to save results of each fold
> results.ICs <- data.frame(matrix(NA, ncol=8, nrow=10))                        # data frame to save results of information criteria
> colnames(results.ICs) <- c("bay.p", "c.hat", "bay.p.cv <http://bay.p.cv>", "c.hat.cv <http://c.hat.cv>", "DIC", "WAIC", "D", "non.convergence")
> for (i in 1:10) {
>   test.indices <- ((i-1)*round(0.1*n.site)+1):(i*round(0.1*n.site))
>   train.indices <- indices[-test.indices]
>
>   inits <- function(){list(N=shuffled.count.initial, alpha.lam=rnorm(1, 0, 1), alpha.p=rnorm(1, 0, 1),
>                            beta.p=rnorm(1, 0, 1), beta1.lam=rnorm(1, 0, 1), beta2.lam=rnorm(1, 0, 1))}
>
>   jags.data <- list(indices=indices, train.indices=train.indices, test.indices=test.indices, n.survey=n.survey,
>                     vege=shuffled.vege, count=shuffled.count)
>
>   out <- jags(jags.data, inits, params, bin.mix, n.chains=nc, n.iter=ni, n.burn = nb, n.thin=nt)
>
>   bay.p <- out$BUGSoutput$mean$bay.p
>   c.hat <- out$BUGSoutput$mean$c.hat
>   bay.p.cv <http://bay.p.cv> <- out$BUGSoutput$mean$bay.p.cv <http://bay.p.cv>
>   c.hat.cv <http://c.hat.cv> <- out$BUGSoutput$mean$c.hat.cv <http://c.hat.cv>
>
>   DIC <- out$BUGSoutput$DIC
>
>   lppd.sum <- -2*sum(log(apply(out$BUGSoutput$sims.list$ppd,2,mean)))
>   pD.2 <- sum(apply(log(out$BUGSoutput$sims.list$ppd), 2, function(x) sd(x)*sd(x)))
>   WAIC <- lppd.sum + pD.2
>
>   count.sim.mean <- apply(out$BUGSoutput$sims.list$count.sim,2,mean)
>   sum1 <- sum((count-count.sim.mean)^2)
>   sum2 <- sum(apply(out$BUGSoutput$sims.list$count.sim,2,function(x) sd(x)*sd(x)))
>   D <- sum1 + sum2
>
>   non.convergence <- length(which(out$BUGSoutput$summary[,8]>1.1))
>
>   results.model[[i]] <- list(summary=data.frame(out$BUGSoutput$summary))
>
>   results.ICs[i,] <- c(bay.p, c.hat, bay.p.cv <http://bay.p.cv>, c.hat.cv <http://c.hat.cv>, DIC, WAIC, D, non.convergence)
>
> }
> end.time = Sys.time()
> elapsed.time = round(difftime(end.time, start.time, units='mins'), dig = 2)
> cat(paste(paste('Posterior models computed in ', elapsed.time, sep=''), ' minutes\n\n', sep=''))
>

messages.body_plain:
You might check out this paper <https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/15-1471.1> (if the link doesn't work, Broms et al. 2016 Model Selection and Assessment for Multispecies occupancy models), which might help you work through some of the issues raised in bullets 2, 3, and 6.

One major difference between logistic regression and N-mix/Occu models is that the latter (as normally implemented in the BUGS language) incorporate latent variables within the likelihood. Apparently (https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/ecs2.1477), WAIC performs better if the likelihood used to estimate pD and the lppd marginalizes over the latent state variables.

Re. 6), I don't know if there are any complete model selection comparisons for estimating trends (one paper I can think of that compares indicator variable selection and out of sample performance with simulated data is https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/ecy.2166). I guess one major consideration that might help limit the scope of any comparison might be whether you are eventually planning to either choose a single "best" model, or average across several models.
